To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the best-fitting factor model of problem behavior for African American adolescents was a bifactor model, (2) the bifactor model included a general factor that accounted for 35% of the variance and 3 correlated specific factors that accounted for 18% of the variance, and (3) the genetic correlations between the general factor and the 3 specific factors were 0.70, 0.69, and 0.72, respectively.

(a) problem behavior in African American adolescents is best described as a bifactor model with general and group-specific factors and (b) genes previously implicated for problem behavior are associated with specific dimensions of problem behavior.

the structure of adolescent problem behavior is best described by a bifactor model, that the bifactor model provides a better representation of genetic associations, and that the genes CHRM2, GABA2, and OPMR1 account for unique variance in problem behaviors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the genetic and environmental factors that influence problem behavior in low-income African American youth.
understanding the genetic and environmental factors that underlie problem behaviors in African American adolescents and the extent to which these factors are shared among behaviors.
the genetic and environmental influences on adolescent problem behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a bifactor model of problem behavior is the best fitting model for the data and is the most appropriate model for future genetic association analyses.

the current study provides the first evidence for the genetic architecture of a multidimensional model of problem behavior among low-income African American youth, with implications for the identification of novel genetic targets for the prevention and treatment of problem behaviors.
the genetic associations for problem behavior are not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic associations with the bifactor model were stronger than those with the traditional unidimensional model.
a bifactor model of problem behavior is a promising approach to understanding the genetic architecture of this phenotype, particularly among low-income African American youth.

a more complex structure of problem behavior is evident among African American adolescents than previously observed, and that genetic association studies should consider the implications of this complexity when evaluating the genetic underpinnings of behavioral covariation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic studies of adolescent behavior would benefit from a more nuanced consideration of phenotypic structure.

a more comprehensive understanding of the structure of problem behaviors and the genetic architecture underlying these phenotypes can be gained by considering both the dimensional complexity of these phenotypes and the potential heterogeneity of the underlying genetic architecture.
genetic association studies of problem behavior should be guided by a thorough understanding of the phenotypic structure of these constructs.
